title: The Gauss–Seidel Iterative Method
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Gauss–Seidel improves on Jacobi by immediately using newly computed components within the same sweep.
short: Update in place rather than waiting for the whole sweep.
long: Update in place rather than waiting for the whole sweep. It often converges about twice as fast as Jacobi for model problems.
proof: The iteration matrix is −(D+L)^{-1}U, and its spectral radius is smaller than that of Jacobi for consistently ordered matrices under standard assumptions.
consequence: It is a classical relaxation method for large sparse systems.

title: Successive Over-Relaxation for Faster Convergence
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: SOR accelerates Gauss–Seidel by extrapolating each correction by a relaxation factor ω, with optimal ω often between one and two.
short: Over-relaxing each correction can dramatically speed up convergence.
long: Over-relaxing each correction can dramatically speed up convergence. For model Poisson problems the optimal factor is roughly 2/(1+sin(pi/(n+1))).
proof: The SOR iteration matrix's spectral radius is minimised at a critical ω, and Young's theorem gives the exact relation to the Jacobi spectral radius for consistently ordered matrices.
consequence: It was a historically important solver for large elliptic PDE discretisations.

title: The Conjugate Gradient Method
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For a symmetric positive definite system, the conjugate gradient method generates mutually A-conjugate search directions and converges in at most n steps in exact arithmetic.
short: Use search directions that do not undo previous progress.
long: Use search directions that do not undo previous progress. In floating point it acts as a fast iterative solver, with convergence governed by the condition number.
proof: Each step minimises the quadratic energy over the current Krylov space; conjugacy makes the minimisations independent, so after n steps the whole space is covered.
consequence: It is the standard iterative solver for large sparse symmetric positive definite systems.

title: GMRES and Krylov Subspace Iterations
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: GMRES solves a nonsymmetric linear system by minimising the residual norm over the Krylov subspace spanned by powers of A applied to the initial residual.
short: Search for the best residual in an expanding Krylov space.
long: Search for the best residual in an expanding Krylov space. Restarting controls memory use at the cost of convergence speed.
proof: Arnoldi iteration builds an orthonormal basis of the Krylov space, reducing the least-squares minimisation to a small upper Hessenberg problem.
consequence: It is a leading method for large nonsymmetric systems arising from discretised PDEs.

title: The QR Algorithm for Computing Eigenvalues
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Repeatedly factoring a matrix as QR and reassembling as RQ produces a sequence of similar matrices converging to upper triangular or Schur form, whose diagonal entries are eigenvalues.
short: Repeated QR factorisations peel off eigenvalues one by one.
long: Repeated QR factorisations peel off eigenvalues one by one. Shifts and implicit bulges accelerate convergence dramatically in practice.
proof: Because A_{k+1}=Q_k^T A_k Q_k, the iterates are unitarily similar and preserve eigenvalues; convergence to Schur form follows from the convergence of subspace iteration.
consequence: It is the standard dense eigenvalue algorithm behind LAPACK.

title: Newton's Method for Nonlinear Systems and the Jacobian
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For a system F(x)=0, Newton's method solves the linearised system J(x_n) δ=−F(x_n) at each step and sets x_{n+1}=x_n+δ.
short: Linearise the system, take one Newton step, and repeat.
long: Linearise the system, take one Newton step, and repeat. Quadratic convergence holds for a nonsingular Jacobian and a good initial guess.
proof: Taylor expanding F about the root and subtracting the Newton correction cancels the linear error term, leaving an error quadratic in the previous one.
consequence: It is the core of nonlinear solvers in scientific computing and optimisation.

title: Lagrange Interpolation Polynomials
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Given n+1 distinct nodes, there is a unique polynomial of degree at most n taking prescribed values at those nodes, expressible as a sum of Lagrange basis polynomials.
short: A basis of polynomials that are one at one node and zero at all others.
long: A basis of polynomials that are one at one node and zero at all others. Newton and barycentric forms are numerically preferable for large n.
proof: Each Lagrange basis polynomial has the required Kronecker delta values at the nodes, so the combination interpolates; uniqueness follows because a degree-n polynomial with n+1 roots is zero.
consequence: It underlies polynomial approximation, quadrature and spectral methods.

title: Newton's Divided Differences for Interpolation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Newton's interpolation form builds the interpolating polynomial incrementally using divided differences, so adding a node requires only one extra term.
short: Compute interpolation coefficients recursively so new data points are cheap to add.
long: Compute interpolation coefficients recursively so new data points are cheap to add. Divided differences converge to derivatives when nodes coalesce.
proof: The recursive definition f[x_0,...,x_k]=(f[x_1,...,x_k]−f[x_0,...,x_{k−1}])/(x_k−x_0) gives coefficients that make the Newton polynomial agree with the Lagrange polynomial at all nodes.
consequence: It is the standard way to update interpolants and derive Hermite interpolation.

title: Cubic Spline Interpolation and Smoothness
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: A cubic spline interpolates data with piecewise cubic polynomials that are twice continuously differentiable at the interior knots, with boundary conditions closing the system.
short: Piecewise cubics give smooth curves without high-degree oscillation.
long: Piecewise cubics give smooth curves without high-degree oscillation. Natural splines impose zero second derivative at the endpoints.
proof: Matching function, first and second derivatives at interior knots gives a tridiagonal linear system for the second derivatives or spline coefficients, which has a unique solution under standard boundary conditions.
consequence: Splines are the default tool for smooth curve fitting in computer graphics and data analysis.

title: Runge's Phenomenon with High-Degree Equispaced Interpolation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Polynomial interpolation at equally spaced nodes can diverge near the endpoints as the degree grows, even for perfectly smooth functions.
short: More equally spaced points can make polynomial interpolation worse.
long: More equally spaced points can make polynomial interpolation worse. The Runge function is the classic example, while Chebyshev nodes cure the problem.
proof: The interpolation error involves the nodal polynomial whose magnitude grows near the endpoints for equispaced nodes, and the Lebesgue constant grows exponentially.
consequence: It motivates Chebyshev nodes, splines and piecewise approximation.

title: The Trapezoidal Rule and Its Error Term
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Approximating the integral by trapezoids gives an error proportional to the square of the subinterval width times the integral of the second derivative.
short: Replace each strip by a trapezoid and get second-order accuracy.
long: Replace each strip by a trapezoid and get second-order accuracy. The composite error is -(b-a)h² f''(ξ)/12 for some ξ in the interval.
proof: On one subinterval, interpolate f linearly and integrate the interpolation error formula, whose leading term involves f''; summing gives the composite error.
consequence: It is the simplest convergent quadrature rule and the basis of Romberg integration.

title: Simpson's Rule and Fourth-Order Accuracy
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Approximating f by a quadratic on each pair of subintervals gives Simpson's rule with error proportional to the fourth power of the subinterval width.
short: Fitting parabolas to pairs of strips buys much higher accuracy.
long: Fitting parabolas to pairs of strips buys much higher accuracy. Simpson's rule is exact for polynomials of degree at most three.
proof: Interpolate f by a quadratic through three nodes on each pair of subintervals and integrate; the leading interpolation error involves f^{(4)} and one additional cancellation raises the degree of exactness.
consequence: It is a widely used default quadrature rule.

title: Gaussian Quadrature and Optimal Node Placement
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: An n-point Gaussian quadrature rule with optimally chosen nodes and weights on an interval is exact for polynomials of degree up to 2n−1.
short: Choosing nodes cleverly doubles the degree of exactness.
long: Choosing nodes cleverly doubles the degree of exactness. The nodes are the roots of the Legendre polynomial of degree n for the uniform weight.
proof: Force exactness on monomials up to degree 2n−1; the nodal polynomial must be orthogonal to all polynomials of degree at most n−1, which characterises it as the corresponding orthogonal polynomial.
consequence: It gives very high accuracy with few function evaluations.

title: Adams–Bashforth Multistep Methods
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Explicit Adams–Bashforth methods advance an ODE solution by integrating an interpolating polynomial through several previous derivative values.
short: Use the history of slopes to extrapolate the next value.
long: Use the history of slopes to extrapolate the next value. They need a one-step method to generate starting values and can have weakened stability for high order.
proof: Replace f in the integral form of the ODE by the polynomial interpolating previous derivative values and integrate that polynomial exactly.
consequence: They are efficient when derivative evaluations dominate cost.

title: Runge–Kutta Methods and Stagewise Accuracy
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Runge–Kutta methods advance an ODE solution by combining several slope evaluations inside a single step to achieve higher order without stored history.
short: Sample the slope several times within each step for higher accuracy.
long: Sample the slope several times within each step for higher accuracy. The classical fourth-order method uses four stages and is the default general-purpose solver.
proof: Match the Taylor expansion of the numerical update to the exact solution's Taylor series up to the desired order, imposing the order conditions on the coefficients.
consequence: They are the most widely used one-step integrators for nonstiff ODEs.

title: A-Stability and Stiff Differential Equations
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: A one-step method is A-stable if its region of absolute stability contains the whole left half-plane, so it remains stable on arbitrarily stiff linear problems.
short: A-stable methods do not impose artificial step-size limits from decaying modes.
long: A-stable methods do not impose artificial step-size limits from decaying modes. The implicit Euler method and the trapezoidal rule are A-stable, while explicit Runge–Kutta methods cannot be.
proof: Apply the method to the scalar test equation y'=λy and analyse the amplification factor R(z) with z=hλ; the stated condition defines A-stability.
consequence: It guides the choice of implicit solvers for stiff systems in chemical and electrical engineering.

title: The Cooley–Tukey FFT and Its Complexity
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The Cooley–Tukey fast Fourier transform computes the discrete Fourier transform of length n in O(n log n) operations by recursively splitting even and odd indices.
short: Divide the DFT into smaller DFTs and recombine with twiddle factors.
long: Divide the DFT into smaller DFTs and recombine with twiddle factors. The radix-2 version requires n to be a power of two, though mixed-radix variants exist.
proof: Separating even and odd indices writes the length-n DFT as two length-n/2 DFTs combined with n complex additions; the recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) gives O(n log n).
consequence: It made digital signal processing, image analysis and fast PDE solvers practical.

title: Finite Difference Discretisations of Partial Differential Equations
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Finite difference methods replace derivatives in a PDE by truncated Taylor-series quotients on a grid, producing a linear or nonlinear system for the grid values.
short: Approximate derivatives by differences of nearby grid values.
long: Approximate derivatives by differences of nearby grid values. The truncation error determines the formal order of accuracy, while stability governs whether errors amplify.
proof: Taylor expand u at neighbouring grid points and subtract to obtain difference quotients with leading error proportional to a power of h.
consequence: They are the oldest and simplest PDE discretisation framework.

title: The CFL Condition for Numerical Stability
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: For an explicit time-stepping scheme on a hyperbolic PDE, stability requires that the physical domain of dependence be contained in the numerical one, typically forcing the time step to be proportional to the spatial mesh width.
short: Information must not travel farther numerically than it does physically.
long: Information must not travel farther numerically than it does physically. The dimensionless ratio is called the Courant number.
proof: For the linear transport equation, von Neumann analysis of the upwind scheme shows that the amplification factor exceeds one in modulus when the Courant number exceeds one.
consequence: It sets the time-step restriction for explicit schemes in fluid dynamics and wave propagation.

title: Gradient Descent and Convex Optimisation
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Gradient descent iteratively moves in the direction of the negative gradient, and for a convex function with Lipschitz gradient a suitable step size gives convergence to a minimiser.
short: Walk downhill repeatedly until the slope vanishes.
long: Walk downhill repeatedly until the slope vanishes. Strong convexity upgrades convergence to a linear rate.
proof: The descent lemma bounds f(x−α∇f) by f(x) minus a positive multiple of the squared gradient norm, so summing shows the gradients tend to zero and convexity gives convergence in function value.
consequence: It is the foundation of machine-learning optimisation and large-scale inverse problems.

title: The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Optimality Conditions
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: Under a constraint qualification, a local optimum of a smooth constrained optimisation problem satisfies stationarity of the Lagrangian, primal feasibility, dual feasibility and complementary slackness.
short: KKT conditions generalise Lagrange multipliers to inequality constraints.
long: KKT conditions generalise Lagrange multipliers to inequality constraints. For convex problems with affine constraints, KKT conditions are also sufficient.
proof: Apply the separating hyperplane theorem to linearised feasible directions, or derive multipliers from the Fritz John conditions and use a constraint qualification to rule out a zero leading multiplier.
consequence: They are the theoretical backbone of constrained optimisation algorithms.

title: Lagrangian Duality and Weak Duality
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The dual of a constrained optimisation problem provides a lower bound on the primal optimum, and under convexity and a constraint qualification strong duality makes the bounds equal.
short: Dual problems give certified bounds and sometimes exact solutions.
long: Dual problems give certified bounds and sometimes exact solutions. The dual variables are the shadow prices of the constraints.
proof: Weak duality follows because the Lagrangian is bounded below by the primal optimum for feasible dual variables; strong duality follows from convex separation under Slater's condition.
consequence: Duality drives interior-point methods and sensitivity analysis in optimisation.

title: The Simplex Method for Linear Programming
subject: Numerical Analysis
statement: The simplex method solves linear programs by moving along edges of the feasible polytope from vertex to vertex, improving the objective until no adjacent vertex is better.
short: Walk around the vertices of the feasible polytope toward better values.
long: Walk around the vertices of the feasible polytope toward better values. It is efficient in practice though Klee–Minty examples show exponential worst-case behaviour.
proof: Each pivot preserves feasibility and improves the objective; since there are finitely many bases, a nondegenerate instance terminates at an optimal vertex, certified by nonnegative reduced costs.
consequence: It revolutionised operations research and underlies many resource-allocation computations.
